Their thesis: the human mind is not a blank slate filled in by culture, but a set of specialised mechanisms, shaped by selection to solve the problems of our hunter-gatherer ancestors. Tooby and Cosmides criticise the "Standard Social Science Model", which puts almost everything on the side of nurture. They also judge the nature/nurture divide false: genes and developmental environments both evolved. For them the mind is made of domain-specific mechanisms rather than a general intelligence.

Pourquoi la raison, propre à l'humain, n: Why does reason, unique to humans, so often lead us to irrational opinions? The authors reject the idea that it mainly serves to understand the world better alone. For them it is a social tool: justifying ourselves, persuading, assessing others' arguments. Used alone, it goes round in circles and can worsen conflicts; in discussion, it corrects itself. They draw on historical examples, everyday anecdotes and experimental psychology. Their theory aims to explain at once why reason evolved, what it does well, and what it cannot do.

Un biologiste de Harvard raconte l'évolu: A Harvard biologist tells the evolution of the human body, from the first bipeds to hunter-gatherers, then farming and industry. Our body, he explains, is poorly suited to the diets and ways of life that culture has produced. Hence "mismatch diseases": obesity, diabetes, heart disease, osteoporosis, linked to processed foods rich in sugar, salt and fat, and to lack of activity. He calls "dysevolution" treating the symptoms of these diseases instead of preventing them, which makes them last. For him, prevention comes first through changing living environments.
